findings.message: copyB: the solver has {days: 3, stops: ['Rome', 'Pisa', 'Bari']}, the execution ends with {days: 3, stops: ['Rome', 'Bari']}
findings.resolution: Not a defect: the question asks for plan, which is {days: 3, stops: ['Rome', 'Pisa']}; line 5 gives copyB its own array, so the solver mis-tracked copyB.

findings.message: The reference is titled 'Exponentiation (**)' and links to the exponentiation page, but the snippet uses only %, *, + and /. A learner who follows 'read more' lands on an operator that is not in the code.
findings.resolution: Fixed: the reference of number-values.parsons-01 now points to the Remainder (%) page, an operator the snippet uses.

findings.message: The explanation says '=== and != both give false here', but != is not one of the chips and is not taught on any card of the unit. The chips that do appear, = and +, are not covered. A learner looks for a chip that is not there.
findings.resolution: Fixed: the explanation now names only the chips that appear (===, = and +) and says what each does, with no mention of !=.

findings.message: Option 3 ('runs once with n equal to 6, because the update comes first') is explained as 'You thought n++ runs before the first test'. Worked through, that belief gives n = 6, the test 6 < 3 fails, and the body never runs, which is the correct answer. The named belief does not produce the option's claim (a pass with n = 6); the option only follows if the test is also skipped, which the feedback does not mention. A learner who holds the belief as described would be led to the right option.
findings.resolution: Fixed: option 3 now states both beliefs (update first and no test on the first pass), and its feedback names both, so the described belief produces the option's claim.

findings.message: The prompt does not say first <= last. If first is greater than last the loop runs zero times, but the reference 'last - first + 1' gives a negative number (first 5, last 3 gives -1). A careful learner may wonder whether to handle that case; the tests never cover it, so the stated 'number of passes' and the reference disagree for some allowed inputs.
findings.resolution: Fixed: the prompt now states that first is never greater than last, so the count last - first + 1 holds for every allowed input.

findings.message: Option 3 ('pour heat pour serve') is attributed to believing a declaration runs its body. Worked through, that belief makes both declarations run: pour prints at its definition, brew runs at its definition (heat, pour, serve), and then the call brew() runs it all again, giving seven lines. The option shows only four lines, so it matches a belief that applies to pour's declaration but not brew's, plus the call. The feedback names only 'runs pour when it is defined', which does not produce this exact value.
findings.resolution: Fixed: option 3 is now the full output of the belief that every definition runs its body (seven lines), and its feedback says both definitions ran before the call.

findings.message: Option 2 feedback says 'The output shows both changes.' The learner is shown only the code, so this states the program's printed result (the assignments take effect), which is the correct option's claim. Feedback may state the one fact the belief missed (const does not lock properties) but not the result.
findings.resolution: Fixed: the wrong option's feedback no longer states the printed result and now only says const does not lock properties and only stops the name being assigned a new object (version 2).

findings.message: Hint 3 says to loop 'with let'. The whole point of the item is choosing let over var, and hint 1 asks exactly which keyword gives each pass its own variable, so hint 3 simply states the keyword to use instead of narrowing toward it.
findings.resolution: Fixed: hint 3 now points at the loop's start value and last pass instead of naming let (version 3).

findings.message: Option 3 ('m is gone after tag returns, so both calls print only hi') does not follow from the belief it encodes. If m really were deleted on return, the inner function would throw a ReferenceError (as the matching option in closure-captures-variable.concept-01 says) or print undefinedhi, never plain hi. The feedback is true but the option's claimed output cannot be produced by the named belief, so it is a muddled distractor.
findings.resolution: Fixed: option 3 now claims calling loud or soft fails, which follows from the belief that m is gone after tag returns (version 2).

findings.message: Feedback for the chip 'this' says the call fails because this.info is not the method. In a browser script, function info is a global property, so this.info() at top level runs and prints 'undefined loaf'; it fails only in module or Node scope. The claim depends on the engine and is not the rule of the language.
findings.resolution: Fixed: the chip 'this' feedback now says only that this does not stand for oat, which holds in every engine and scope (version 3).

findings.message: The feedback of the option 'Each spread starts a fresh count...' says 'Ask what [Symbol.iterator] returns on line 2'. Line 2 is 'const laps = {'; the [Symbol.iterator] method is on line 3. The learner is sent to the wrong line.
findings.resolution: Fixed: the feedback now points to line 3, where [Symbol.iterator] is defined (version 4).

findings.message: The feedback of 'Uncaught TypeError' says the learner believed the new name stands on the left of the colon, 'so head is undefined'. Working that belief through { first: head, last } = bus: the variable first would take bus.head (undefined), and no variable called head would exist at all. console.log(head(), last()) would then throw an Uncaught ReferenceError, not a TypeError. The named belief (rename-direction-reversed) does not produce the option's value, and the feedback describes head as undefined when it would be an undeclared name.
findings.resolution: Fixed: the wrong option is now 'Uncaught ReferenceError' with feedback matching the reversed-rename belief (no head variable exists), version 4.

findings.message: The reference points to the Exponentiation (**) page, but the snippet uses only *, /, % and +. The pointer leads the learner to an operator that appears nowhere in the item.
findings.resolution: Fixed: same defect as finding 1, the reference now points to the Remainder (%) page.

findings.message: Hint 3 says to use the property the lesson card shows on "tea", but the card gives no such example: it names the length property in one sentence and shows toUpperCase() with no "tea" string. The hint points at something that is not on the card.
findings.resolution: Not a defect: the lesson-2 card's worked example shows "tea".length, so hint 3 does point at something on the card.

findings.message: The answer depends on + turning undefined into the word undefined when joined to text (and the lesson's write-02 and predict items rely on the same for null). The earlier unit taught only that a number and a boolean become text under +, and this lesson's card says nothing about joining undefined or null. The learner has no taught rule for the join, only the hint in this item.
findings.resolution: Fixed: the undefined-and-null card now says that joined to text with + each becomes its own word, and its worked example prints "Seat: undefined".

findings.message: The explanation says "=== and != both give false here", but != is not a chip of this item and is taught nowhere (the unit teaches === and !==, and == on the card). The explanation names an operator the learner has never been given.
findings.resolution: Fixed: same defect as finding 2, the explanation no longer mentions != and describes the chips that exist.

findings.message: Rated 1, the Beginner lower step, but the learner must follow four loop turns (w = 1 to 4), each changing points (10, 30, 60, 100), and combine the accumulator with the precedence of w * 10. Four or more loop turns is the upper step, 2.
findings.resolution: Fixed: the loop now runs three turns (w = 1 to 3, starting from 5), with the answer 65 and options, feedback and explanation updated, so rating 1 holds.

findings.message: Rated 1, the Beginner lower step, but the loop turns five times (row = 0 to 4) with a continue on one of them, so the learner follows five loop turns and a skipped print. Four or more loop turns is the upper step, 2.
findings.resolution: Fixed: the loop now runs three turns (row < 3, continue on row 1), printing 0 and 2, with options, hint and explanation updated, so rating 1 holds.

findings.message: The function body reads and assigns a variable declared outside it (laps), so the learner must know a function can reach an outer variable. No earlier unit and no card of this unit teaches that; the card says only that a function is a named block that runs on a call. The same gap applies to parsons-01 (bump changes the outer n).
findings.resolution: Fixed: the functions lesson-1 card now says a function can read and change a variable declared outside it, and its worked example shows that.

findings.message: Rated 2, the Intermediate lower step, but reaching the second run of line 5 means following four callback calls (38 and 40 skip the if, 42 and 44 pass) with a conditional on each, plus a second idea (an if inside the callback). That is four or more calls to follow: the upper step, 3.
findings.resolution: Fixed: difficulty raised from 2 to 3 because four callback calls with a conditional must be followed (version 3).

findings.message: Rated 2, the Intermediate lower step, but it combines two rules of the concept (a function declaration is ready early; a var holding a function is undefined until its line) with a third idea, that calling undefined throws a TypeError, which neither the card nor a declared prerequisite teaches. That is the upper step, 3. The same TypeError rule is also the answer's key fact and is not taught before this lesson.
findings.resolution: Fixed: the snippet now prints a hoisted var (undefined) instead of calling it, so the item needs no TypeError rule and stays at 2; option 3 uses var-hoisted-with-value and the unused function-expression-hoisted-like-declaration misconception was removed (version 8).

findings.message: Promise.resolve is needed to read this snippet (and Promise.reject in promise-basics.concept-01 and the later async items), but the lesson 2 card teaches only then, catch and new Promise(fn), and no earlier unit covers promises. The static helpers that make an already fulfilled or rejected promise are not taught anywhere before their first use.
findings.resolution: Fixed: the lesson 2 card now says Promise.resolve(v) and Promise.reject(r) make an already settled promise.

findings.message: The answer depends on the rule that a throw inside an async function becomes a rejection of the returned promise. Neither card teaches it: lesson 3 says only that an async function returns a promise, and lesson 4 covers the other direction (an awaited rejection throws). The rule appears only in the explanation and feedback. async-error-handling.fix-01 relies on the same untaught rule (checkSoil throws inside an async function).
findings.resolution: Fixed: the lesson 3 card now says a throw inside an async function rejects the promise it returns.

findings.message: The answer rests on the fact that querySelectorAll returns a NodeList that has forEach but no map. The lesson 1 card says only that querySelectorAll returns all matches, and no earlier unit covers the DOM. The learner never sees the output (CONCEPT_MCQ), so the claim cannot be worked out from the card; it is stated only in the explanation and feedback.
findings.resolution: Fixed: the lesson 1 card now says querySelectorAll returns a NodeList that has forEach but no map.

findings.message: The correct answer depends on classList.add skipping a class the element already has, so className is 'big' and not 'big big'. The lesson 2 card says add changes one class and leaves the others, but never says a repeated add does nothing. The rule appears only in the explanation and feedback.
findings.resolution: Fixed: the lesson 2 card now says adding a class already present changes nothing.

findings.message: Rated 2, the Intermediate lower step, but the correct program takes five changes of state (page, h2, then three edits to the heading text: assignment, += ' (3)', += '!') and the learner must order two += pieces against each other. That is four or more changes of state: the upper step, 3, which is what dom-tree-and-selection.parsons-01 is given for a shorter chain.
findings.resolution: Fixed: difficulty raised from 2 to 3 (five changes of state, two += pieces to order), version 2.

findings.message: Rated 4, the Advanced upper step, but it applies one rule directly: a WeakMap key must be an object (crate.id is a string, so the object itself is the key). That is the same single rule, with the same two changes of state, as predict-01 of this lesson, which is rated 3. It combines no second idea and needs no four-step trace: lower step, 3.
findings.resolution: Fixed: fix-01 re-rated from 4 to 3 (single rule, same step as predict-01), version bumped; the lesson's last item write-01 stays at 4.

findings.message: Rated 3, the Advanced lower step (at most three changes of state), but the learner must follow three scheduled calls at 0, 100 and 400 ms, a clearTimeout that cancels the pending timer at 100, two timer firings at 300 and 600, and the shared variable t reassigned on each call. That is five or more changes across queued callbacks and a cancellation, plus the closure-private-state idea: the upper step, 4.
findings.resolution: Fixed: instead of re-rating (which would break the in-lesson floor), predict-01 now has only two calls (0 and 100 ms) so it needs three changes of state and stays at 3; options, hints and explanation rewritten, version bumped, and the now-unused misconception debounce-ignores-gap replaced by first-call-wins.

findings.message: Rated 4, the Expert lower step (one idea, at most three changes of state), but it asks the learner to write a round-robin simulation: a queue of job objects, shift and push back, a per-job step counter and a termination test, with the tests running five or six turns. The async idea (calls take turns after each await) is combined with a second idea, queue bookkeeping across many loop turns: the upper step, 5, like the chunk item of lesson 1.
findings.resolution: Fixed: write-02 re-rated from 4 to 5 (async idea plus queue bookkeeping over many turns); it is the lesson's last item, so the in-lesson rule holds, version bumped.

findings.message: Rated 4, the Expert lower step (one idea), but three blanks need the lesson's idea (pass functions in, not their results) combined with an earlier concept, this-lost-and-bound, declared as a prerequisite: the learner must reject the bare lines.push chip because a detached method loses its array and accept the wrapper arrow. Passing the three roles also takes tracing a call chain through report. Two ideas: the upper step, 5.
findings.resolution: Fixed: fill-01 re-rated from 4 to 5 (two ideas combined: pass roles in plus this-lost-and-bound); it is the lesson's last item, so the in-lesson rule holds, version bumped.
